chapters.title: Chapter 7: KYC, Demat Rules and Avoiding Common Mistakes

lessons.title: Building a Simple Year-End Tax Checklist for Your Portfolio

body.text: Everything in this course fits onto one calendar. The investors who never get an unpleasant surprise aren't the ones who know more tax law, they're the ones who touch the same few things at the same points in the year, every year.

children.text: This final lesson turns everything covered across this course into one repeatable annual routine, anchored to the dates that actually matter.

events.title: New Financial Year Begins
events.description: Start a simple running log of every capital gain, dividend and interest payout as it happens, rather than reconstructing it all at filing time (Chapter 1).

events.title: First Advance Tax Instalment (15%)
events.description: If your estimated tax liability for the year crosses the advance tax threshold, pay at least 15% of it by this date.

events.title: Second Advance Tax Instalment (45% Cumulative)
events.description: Reassess your estimated liability, including any large gains or dividends received since April, and true up to 45% cumulative.

events.title: Third Advance Tax Instalment (75% Cumulative)
events.description: True up to 75% cumulative, factoring in the specific relief for capital gains and dividend income covered in Chapters 2 and 4.

events.title: Belated Return Deadline (Prior Year)
events.description: Typically the last chance to file a late return for the previous financial year. After this, filing becomes considerably harder.

events.title: Fourth and Final Advance Tax Instalment (100%)
events.description: True up to your full estimated liability for the year.

events.title: Financial Year Ends
events.description: Do a full reconciliation pass: dividends, interest, capital gains, and any losses to carry forward.

events.title: ITR Filing Due Date
events.description: File your return, after completing the reconciliation and Schedule CG walkthrough from Chapter 5.

body.text: The advance tax instalment dates and percentages have been stable for many years. The ITR filing due date, though, is sometimes extended by the CBDT in a given year. Confirm both against the income tax portal each year rather than assuming this calendar is exact for the year you're actually filing in.

children.text: Five Things Worth Checking at Least Once a Year, Regardless of Date
Not everything in this course ties to a specific date. Some things just need to happen at least once a year, on their own schedule.

body.title: Annual Housekeeping, Not Tied to a Specific Date
steps: Confirm your PAN is still linked to Aadhaar and hasn't lapsed into inoperative status (Chapter 1)
Review your KYC status across every broker and fund house, especially accounts you rarely use (Chapter 7)
Confirm your nomination is still current and reflects who you actually want to receive your holdings (Chapter 7)
Claim any dividends sitting unclaimed before they edge closer to the 7-year IEPF transfer window (Chapter 1)
Pull Form 26AS and AIS at least once mid-year, not just right before filing, to catch mismatches early (Chapter 4)

children.text: Putting It Together: A Full-Year Example
This course has covered a lot of individual rules across seven chapters. Here's what it looks like when one investor actually lives through a full year with them.

body.title: A Full Year, Start to Finish
body.scenario: An investor sold equity mutual fund units in August, realizing a ₹2,00,000 long-term capital gain. She continued receiving dividends throughout the year, and has a ₹15,000 short-term capital loss carried forward from two years ago, from a year in which she filed her ITR on time.
body.prompt: Walk through, in order, what she should do across the rest of the financial year.
body.modelAnswer: First, she logs the August LTCG in her running record immediately, rather than waiting until filing season (Chapter 1). Since this ₹2,00,000 gain likely pushes her past the advance tax threshold, she factors it into her 15 September instalment, benefiting from the same relief covered in Chapter 4 that excuses any earlier-quarter shortfall on unpredictable income like capital gains, as long as she pays by the instalment following the quarter she actually sold. She keeps logging dividends as they arrive through the rest of the year. Her ₹15,000 brought-forward short-term capital loss can be set off against this long-term gain, since short-term losses can offset both short-term and long-term gains (Chapter 2), reducing her taxable LTCG. Partway through the year, she pulls Form 26AS and AIS to check her dividend and mutual fund records against what's been reported (Chapter 4). At year-end, she does a full reconciliation, then files using ITR-2, entering the mutual fund gain in Schedule CG, and Schedule 112A if it qualifies under Section 112A, by the due date, having already handled her advance tax through the year rather than facing one large, unplanned bill at filing time.

body.label: One Calendar, Seven Chapters
body.context: Every rule in this course eventually reduces to a handful of habits, repeated on a predictable annual rhythm, not a pile of facts to relearn from scratch each filing season.

body.title: Course Glossary: The Terms Worth Remembering Most

cards.definition: ₹1.25 lakh exempt annually on long-term equity and equity mutual fund gains, taxed at 12.5% above that, as of the rules covered in Chapter 2.
The rule treating the oldest surviving lot in a demat account as sold first, applied separately per account.
The tax department's own record of what's been deducted and reported against your PAN, essential to reconcile before filing.
Quarterly payments (15%, 45%, 75%, 100% cumulative) due through the year on estimated tax liability above the threshold.
The ITR form most investors in this course will need, covering capital gains of any amount without business income.
A mandatory declaration on every demat account and mutual fund folio, facilitating transfer of holdings, though not overriding succession law.

points: The investor tax calendar runs from 1 April through the ITR filing due date, with four advance tax checkpoints along the way
A handful of housekeeping checks, PAN-Aadhaar linking, KYC, nomination, unclaimed dividends, and AIS reconciliation, aren't tied to a specific date but deserve at least one pass a year
Reconciling as you go, rather than reconstructing everything at filing time, is the single habit that ties every chapter of this course together
Capital gains, dividends, TDS, regulatory protections and compliance mechanics all reduce to a repeatable annual routine, not a one-time study exercise
Tax rules and thresholds shift with each Union Budget, so this course is a foundation to build annual habits on, not a substitute for checking current figures each year
